teaching.causalExplanation: Start with momentum. In Year 11, momentum is mass times velocity, and force is the rate of change of momentum, F equals delta p over delta t. So a steady force adds the same momentum every second. Ten thousand newtons adds ten thousand kilogram metres per second of momentum, each second. That rule still holds near the speed of light. What changes is how momentum depends on speed. To keep momentum conserved in every inertial frame, Einstein showed that it has to be p equals m zero v, over the square root of one minus v squared over c squared. That's gamma, times m zero v. Here m zero is the rest mass, the mass measured when the object is at rest. At everyday speeds gamma is one, so this is just m v. Near the speed of light, gamma gets huge. Plot momentum against speed. The classical line, m v, is straight, and reaches m zero c at the speed of light, nothing special. The relativistic curve starts on that line at low speed, then bends upwards, and climbs without limit as v approaches c. It never touches the line where v equals c.

- **Learner question (route wording kept).** "Why does ever more momentum fail to push mass to light speed?" The answer, built in order: a steady force always adds momentum at a steady rate (2); relativistic momentum is γm₀v, which grows without limit as v approaches c (3, 4); so steady pushing raises momentum forever while the speed only creeps towards c, and reaching c would need infinite momentum (5, 6).
- **Hook (new; owner "real context", route "start from the physical case").** An idealised probe: 1000 kg, thrust 1.0 × 10⁴ N, fuel use ignored (tag "idealised: constant mass"). - **Force and momentum (Year 11 recall).** F = Δp/Δt holds in relativity (author note b); a steady force adds a fixed momentum each second.
- **Relativistic momentum (data-sheet form p_v = m₀v/√(1 − v²/c²)).** The reason it must change is given in one sentence: momentum conservation must hold in every inertial frame (postulate 1, v12), and with relativistic time and length mv would not be conserved in all frames; γm₀v is (author note c). - **Graph (site Figure 1 adapted from kinetic energy to momentum; kit `m7-energy` "curve stops below c; infinity is not a plotted data point").** p/(m₀c) against v/c: classical straight line to 1 at v = c; relativistic curve with a vertical asymptote at v = c.

scenes.teachingReason: What changes is how momentum depends on speed. To keep momentum conserved in every inertial frame, Einstein showed that it has to be p equals m zero v, over the square root of one minus v squared over c squared. That's gamma, times m zero v. Here m zero is the rest mass, the mass measured when the object is at rest. At everyday speeds gamma is one, so this is just m v. Near the speed of light, gamma gets huge.

scenes.teachingReason: Particle accelerators depend on this every day. Remember, a charged particle in a magnetic field moves in a circle of radius p over q B, and the momentum in that formula has to be gamma m zero v. At CERN's Large Hadron Collider, protons travel within about three metres per second of the speed of light, with gamma near seven thousand. Its bending magnets curve them on a radius of nearly three kilometres. If momentum were just m v, the same magnets would bend them in a circle of radius about forty centimetres.

So how does mass-energy accounting explain fusion, annihilation and combustion?
